hints: Focus on what each definition actually produces, atoms, ions or electrons, not just what it starts with.
Write the first ionisation equation in your head as $\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+(\text{g}) + \text{e}^-$ and ask if a positive ion appears.
Compare heterolytic fission which splits both electrons to one atom, with atomisation which just makes neutral gaseous atoms, to see which one must make a cation.
walkthrough:
**Recall first ionisation energy**

Think of removing one electron from a neutral gaseous atom. That must leave a positive ion behind.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+(\text{g}) + \text{e}^-$$

**Recall heterolytic fission**

Think of a covalent bond breaking unevenly, so both shared electrons go to one atom. That gives one positive ion and one negative ion.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{H-Br} \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{Br}^-$$

**Recall enthalpy change of atomisation**

Think of making separate neutral gaseous atoms from an element. No electrons are lost or gained, so no ions are formed.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Na(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na(g)}$$

**Combine the conclusions**

Statements 1 and 2 both include formation of a positive ion, but statement 3 gives only neutral atoms. So 1 and 2 only is the correct combination.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes statement 3. Enthalpy change of atomisation forms neutral gaseous atoms, for example $\text{Cl}_2$ to $2\text{Cl(g)}$, with no positive ion formed.
options.B: Correct because 1 and 2 both form a positive ion. First ionisation energy forms $\text{X}^+(\text{g}) + \text{e}^-$, and heterolytic fission forms a cation plus an anion, for example $\text{H}^+ + \text{Br}^-$.
options.C: Incorrect because it includes 3 but omits 1. Statement 1 clearly forms $\text{X}^+$, while statement 3 does not form any ion.
options.D: Incorrect because it includes only 1. It correctly recognises first ionisation energy but misses that heterolytic fission also produces a positive ion alongside a negative ion.
